stories.headline: South Korea Proposes Official Talks to End Korean War
stories.summary:
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung used Liberation Day ceremonies on Saturday to formally propose peace talks with North Korea aimed at officially ending the Korean War, which has remained technically active under a 1953 armistice. Lee called for a "multi-layered security system" to reduce tensions along the demilitarized zone and offered to discuss practical measures to halt North Korea's nuclear program.

Lee, who came to power after his predecessor Yoon Suk Yeol was impeached for attempting to declare martial law, has pursued a policy of engagement with Pyongyang and Beijing. He told the ceremony the two nations should "put down our intentions to threaten each other" and sit face-to-face for discussions on peaceful coexistence, while acknowledging that full denuclearization remains a long-term goal and a freeze on nuclear production a more realistic near-term objective.

North Korea has not yet responded to the overture. The proposal comes just days after Pyongyang fired a ballistic missile into the sea — its 11th suspected test this year — and North Korean state media made no mention of Lee's offer, instead covering Kim Jong Un's own Liberation Day commemorations. Pyongyang has previously rejected Lee's outreach, criticizing US-South Korean military cooperation agreements.

The initiative carries geopolitical weight as President Trump, the only Western leader to have met Kim Jong Un, has expressed renewed interest in engagement with the North Korean leader. Lee has indicated he would support a Trump-Kim deal to freeze nuclear production as a step toward denuclearization.

stories.headline: Record Heat Wave Sears Europe; Deadly Floods Hit Japan and Midwest
stories.summary:
A record-breaking heat wave driven in part by human-caused climate change is sweeping across Europe, with Belgium logging its highest temperature of the summer on Friday. Drought-stricken fields and fast-spreading wildfires have challenged firefighters across the continent; at least one person was killed in Croatia after an overnight blaze engulfed homes and vehicles, and fires also swept parts of the United Kingdom.

In Japan, record-breaking rainfall — roughly three months' worth in 12 hours — triggered severe flooding across multiple cities east of Tokyo, killing at least five people and stranding thousands who spent the night in airports and train stations. Stormwater submerged cars and railway tracks; authorities warned that more rain is forecast even as floodwaters began to recede.

In the United States, approximately 20 million Americans remain under flood watches in parts of Indiana, Illinois, and Ohio following six days of heavy rain, with multiple communities evacuated. Meanwhile, the National Weather Service warns dangerous heat will persist through the weekend across the Southern Plains and Lower Mississippi Valley, where humidity-adjusted temperatures could reach 115 degrees Fahrenheit.

Hawaii faces an additional threat: Tropical Storm Lala is expected to strengthen into a hurricane before reaching the Big Island this weekend. The National Hurricane Center has issued hurricane warnings; the storm could drop up to 25 inches of rain and bring the risk of mudslides and rip currents.

stories.headline: Kennedy Center Board Votes to Put Trump's Name on Facade, Defying Court Order
stories.summary:
The Kennedy Center's board of trustees voted Thursday to add the inscription "Restored and Renovated By President Donald J. Trump" to the institution's facade and rename the plaza outside "the President Donald J. Trump Plaza" — moves that appear designed to circumvent a federal court ruling that had blocked Trump's name from being added to the center's official title.

U.S. District Court Judge Christopher Cooper, appointed by President Obama, ruled in late May that the board had exceeded its authority when it unanimously voted in December to rename the center "The Donald J. Trump and The John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts," finding that congressional approval is required for an official name change. The board also voted Thursday to close most of the center for two years for renovations — another action Cooper had blocked.

Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-OH), who sits on the board and brought the original lawsuit challenging the name change, said the Thursday vote sought to "circumvent" Cooper's ruling. Her attorneys, Norm Eisen and Nathaniel Zelinsky, called the vote "a show of blatant disrespect to the courts" and said the defendants would face renewed legal challenge.

The episode sets up a fresh courtroom confrontation over the limits of executive and institutional authority versus judicial orders. Supporters of the renovation argue Trump's substantial personal and political investment in the center's overhaul warrants formal recognition; critics contend the board is acting in defiance of clear judicial direction.

stories.headline: DNC Chair Warns Party Faces Severe Fundraising Gap Ahead of Midterms
stories.summary:
Democratic National Committee Chairman Ken Martin told an executive committee meeting Friday that while the DNC has raised a record amount in the 198-year history of the organization, it still faces a dire financial disadvantage against Republicans heading into the November midterm elections. Martin urged allies to increase contributions in the final months before Election Day, warning that "we need more" despite the record haul.

The financial disparity is stark at the party-committee level: the DNC ended June with just $16.3 million cash on hand and more than $18 million in debt, compared to the Republican National Committee's $129 million. On the congressional side, the NRCC held nearly $93 million and the NRSC $56 million, while their Democratic counterparts — the DCCC with $73 million and DSCC with $41 million — trail but by narrower margins. President Trump's super PAC, MAGA Inc., separately holds a $400 million war chest, though it has not yet deployed significant spending.

Martin attributed the imbalance in part to Republican incumbency advantages, saying the White House has "auctioned off the federal government" and is "getting their war chest filled by every corporation under the sun" — a characterization Republicans reject, arguing their fundraising reflects broad grassroots and donor enthusiasm for Trump's agenda.

Individual Democratic Senate candidates are faring considerably better. Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA) had $42 million on hand at the end of June, dwarfing his Republican opponent's $2.2 million, and Democrats hold similar leads in other key Senate contests including North Carolina. Strategists on both sides say the candidate-level money may partially offset the national committee gap, though the overall environment favors Republicans.

stories.headline: Jason Arday, Ex-Cambridge Professor at Center of Plagiarism Row, Found Dead
stories.summary:
Jason Arday, 41, who resigned last week as a University of Cambridge professor of sociology of education amid plagiarism allegations, has been found dead at an address in Battersea, south London. Emergency services found a man unresponsive Friday afternoon; the Metropolitan Police said the death is being treated as unexpected but not suspicious.

Arday had denied plagiarism allegations, acknowledging errors in his work but attributing some to his autism. He had said the controversy — which erupted after academic Nathan Cofnas published claims of numerous instances of plagiarism — had caused 'an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack.' Arday's family said in a statement that 'the campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason,' describing him as a 'gentle man who always wanted to see the best in everyone.'

Arday became Cambridge's youngest-ever Black professor at 37 in 2023, a moment widely described as a milestone. Cambridge vice-chancellor Prof. Deborah Prentice called the news 'desperately saddening,' and UK Education Secretary Lucy Powell urged people to 'remember there are real people with loved ones involved.' The circumstances of his death have prompted renewed public debate about the conduct of academic and online scrutiny.

stories.headline: Phoenix Air Traffic Controller Averts Potential Disaster After Two American Airlines Jets Share Same Flight Number
stories.summary:
A Phoenix air traffic controller averted a potential mid-air collision early Friday after two American Airlines aircraft were mistakenly assigned the same flight number — American 2482 — and briefly shared the same airspace. Audio of the incident, posted by ATC.com, captured the controller distinguishing between 'American 2482 on the arrival' and 'American 2482 on the departure' to prevent dangerous confusion over altitude directives.

The duplication occurred because a Chicago-bound flight was delayed by weather, prompting American to dispatch a second plane from Phoenix on the same route. With both aircraft aloft simultaneously, a dispatcher failure to catch the overlap in flight planning meant both pilots were operating under the same call sign. Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo, who has four decades of airline experience, said such incidents are extremely rare and praised the system's built-in redundancy.

The Federal Aviation Administration and American Airlines both confirmed they will investigate how the error occurred. The controller, who said he had never seen two aircraft 'pretty much merge with the same call sign' in 25 years, was complimented by one of the pilots for his 'nice work.' The incident comes amid ongoing national scrutiny of air traffic control staffing and aviation safety procedures.

stories.headline: Abbott Directs Grant Review Over DFW Airport Islamic Washing Facilities; Airport Drops Plan
stories.summary:
Texas Gov. Greg Abbott on Friday directed a review of state grants to entities operating Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport and George Bush Intercontinental Airport in Houston, citing religious accommodation concerns, and referred both airports to the U.S. Department of Transportation for investigation. The action came after DFW announced it would not proceed with a proposal to install Islamic ablution washing stations on the pre-security side of its international terminal.

Abbott wrote on X that 'government-owned airports cannot favor one religion over all others,' calling the DFW plan illegal. DFW said it had been evaluating the proposal and determined not to proceed after accelerated review, citing that the project 'would not deliver the originally anticipated operational benefits.' The airport had previously said details in a contractor filing — including a $300,000 cost estimate and a 'privately funded' designation — resulted from administrative errors by an outside design firm.

Supporters of the original plan argued that ablution facilities serve a broad international traveling public and that comparable amenities for other religious practices exist in airports globally, framing the accommodation as neutral customer service rather than religious favoritism. Critics, including Abbott, contend that installing faith-specific facilities at taxpayer-funded airports violates the constitutional principle of government neutrality toward religion. The episode reflects a broader national debate over religious accommodations in public spaces.

stories.headline: Builders Unearth €9 Million Gold Stash Hidden in Walls of Belgian Property
stories.summary:
Construction workers renovating a property in East Flanders, Belgium, discovered a trove of gold bars and coins estimated at €9 million sealed inside the cellar walls earlier this week. The find, made while drilling for new sewage pipes, is believed to be one of the largest such discoveries in recent Belgian history.

The property belongs to CAW Oost-Vlaanderen, a welfare charity in Dendermonde. Its director said he hopes the gold might eventually support the charity's work. Police have secured the hoard and warned the public against visiting the site. Under Belgian law, a rightful owner has five years to come forward; if no claim is established, proceeds are divided between the finder and the property owner — provided the stash is not linked to criminal activity.

Local prosecutors have launched an investigation into the origin of the gold. The incident has drawn international attention and raised legal questions about treasure ownership under Belgian civil law.
